_readme: U14 — comparison, degree and the language of describing data. Seven points, band 3400-3499.
gr_change_language and gr_multiples carry Academic Task 1 almost on their own; gr_comparative_grading is the hedging layer between a band 6 and a band 7 description.
Two points are role: choice (gr_comparative_grading, gr_multiples). Both sit in cs_quantifier_polarity and share the board gb_grading_vs_multiples.

points.title: Saying that one thing is bigger, quicker or better than another

point_json.grammar_name: Comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs

teach.can_do: I can say that one thing is bigger, quicker or better than another, and which one is the best of a group.
teach.why_it_matters: Every chart description and half of every opinion paragraph is built out of these endings, and the two ways of breaking them are visible from across the room.
teach.meaning: A comparison puts two things on one scale and says which of them sits higher. It does not say by how much, and it does not say either of them is high — a slower train can still be fast. The top form does something different again: it takes one thing out of a named group and puts it at the end of the scale, with nothing left beyond it. That is a much stronger claim, and it is the one a reader will check.

form.pattern: SHORT WORD + -er + than  ·  more + LONG WORD + than  ·  the + -est  ·  the most + LONG WORD
notes: one syllable: add -er and -est — fast, faster, the fastest
one syllable ending consonant-vowel-consonant: double the last letter — big, bigger, the biggest; hot, hotter, the hottest. Not after w, x or y: new, newer; slow, slower
ending in -e: add -r and -st only — safe, safer, the safest; large, larger, the largest
two syllables ending in -y: the y becomes i — busy, busier, the busiest; early, earlier, the earliest
two syllables or more otherwise: more and the most — careful, more careful, the most careful
a handful of two-syllable words take either: quiet, clever, narrow, simple, gentle — quieter or more quiet, both fine

words describing how something is done and ending in -ly take more and the most: more quickly, the most carefully. But fast, hard, early, late, soon and long keep the ending: arrives earliest, works hardest

the ones that ignore all of this: good and well go to better and the best; bad and badly go to worse and the worst; far goes to further or farther and the furthest or the farthest; little goes to less and the least; much and many both go to more and the most
never both at once: not more easier, not the most biggest
the goes in front of every top form — the cheapest fares, not cheapest fares
form.negative: less + word + than sends the comparison the other way: the new timetable is less reliable than the old one.
form.question: Which route is quicker, the coast road or the bypass?

spec.label: how long does the crossing take?

steps.gloss: the quickest of the three; nothing in the group beats it
quicker than the coast road, slower than the tunnel

worked_example.sentence: The bypass is quicker than the coast road, but the tunnel is the quickest of the three.
worked_example.why_this_form: The first half weighs two roads against each other and names the winner. The second half stops weighing and ranks: nothing in the group is left above the tunnel.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Write that the tunnel is quicker and you have beaten one rival only. The -est ending is what puts it in front of every crossing in the group.

notice_set.sentence: The 8:10 is slower than the 8:40.
notice_set.question: Which train takes longer to get there?
notice_set.why: Slower puts the 8:10 lower on the speed scale, and than names the train it is being measured against.

notice_set.sentence: The Verdon bridge is the narrowest crossing on the river.
notice_set.question: How many crossings on the river are narrower?
notice_set.why: The -est ending puts the bridge at the end of the line, so there is nothing left below it in that group.

notice_set.sentence: Fares on the coast route rose more steeply than fares on the bypass.
notice_set.question: Where did people end up paying a bigger increase?
notice_set.why: More steeply measures the two rises against each other, and the coast route is the one placed higher.

notice_set.sentence: This lift is less reliable than the one in the north block.
notice_set.question: Which lift breaks down more often?
options: the one in the north block
notice_set.why: Less sends the comparison downwards, so this lift sits below the other one on the reliability scale.

notice_set.sentence: Halima cycles further to work than anyone else on her floor.
notice_set.question: Does anybody on her floor have a longer ride in?
notice_set.why: Anyone else sweeps in the whole floor, so beating all of them leaves nobody with a longer journey.

discovery.prompt: The describing words on the left change their ending. The ones on the right take an extra word in front instead. Work out what decides it.
pairs: The path is more crowded here.
Fares are more affordable this year.

candidate_rules.text: Short words change their ending; longer words take an extra word in front.
Words about size and speed change their ending.
Add -er whenever the sentence contains than.

teach.rule_line: Count the syllables: one takes the ending, three or more take more, two can go either way.
teach.false_rule: That more is the polite or academic way of building a comparison. It is not a style choice at all — the length of the word decides it for you.

errors.wrong: The coast road is more quicker than the bypass at that hour.
errors.right: The coast road is quicker than the bypass at that hour.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has two working ways of building a comparison and no rule for choosing between them, so both go in for safety. Doubling up feels like emphasis rather than like an error.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: more.

errors.wrong: The Verdon is the most long river in the county.
errors.right: The Verdon is the longest river in the county.
errors.why_it_happens: Most is easier to reach for than a spelling change, and it works on almost every word the learner has met in an essay. Nothing warns them that a one-syllable word refuses it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: most long becomes longest.

errors.wrong: The new lifts run more quick than the old ones.
errors.right: The new lifts run more quickly than the old ones.
errors.why_it_happens: The word is describing how the lifts run rather than what they are like, and that difference is invisible until somebody points at it. The comparison itself was built correctly.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: quick becomes quickly.

errors.wrong: Sandmouth has cheapest fares anywhere on this stretch of coast.
errors.right: Sandmouth has the cheapest fares anywhere on this stretch of coast.
errors.why_it_happens: The ending already feels like it has done the ranking, so the small word in front looks like it is not carrying anything. In this one place it is compulsory.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: the.

pays_in.note: The overview sentence ranks the bars, and ranking is what these endings are for.
pays_in.model: Road carried more freight than rail and water combined throughout the period.

pays_in.note: Questions about your town, your commute or your job all invite a comparison.
pays_in.model: The bus is cheaper, but the train gets me in a good deal earlier.

pays_in.note: A statement that quietly upgrades a comparison into a top ranking is false on one ending.
pays_in.model: Sandmouth recorded the steepest fall of the four coastal towns.

used_in.quote: Three lines on one graph cannot be described without ranking them, and ranking three things needs both the two-way and the top form.
Answers about a home town turn into comparisons with somewhere else within about two sentences.

payload.sentence: The bypass is busier than the coast road at this time of day.
payload.question: Which road has more traffic on it right now?

feedback.why_key: Busier puts the bypass higher on one scale, and than names the road it has been measured against.
feedback.feed_forward: Read than as the thing that came second.

payload.sentence: Sandmouth had the lowest rents of the four districts surveyed.
payload.question: How many of the four districts were cheaper than Sandmouth?

feedback.why_key: The ending places Sandmouth at the bottom of a named group, so nothing inside that group sits below it.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat an -est ending as a claim about the whole group.

payload.context: A first draft describing a graph of journey times.
payload.sentence: Travel by rail became more quicker across the ten-year period.
reasons: the comparison has been built twice over
the wrong two things are being weighed
the period named is too long for this word
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Quicker has already done the whole job. More tries to do it a second time and English allows only one of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Use more or use the ending, never both.

payload.context: A note attached to a table of district rents.
payload.stem: Rents in Ashfield are ___ (high) than anywhere else along the line.

feedback.why_key: One syllable, so the ending carries the comparison and there is nothing for an extra word to do.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the syllables before you reach for more.

payload.context: Two runners weighing up two ways round the park.
payload.stem: The river loop is ___ (muddy) in winter than the path along the top.

feedback.why_key: Two syllables ending in y, so the y turns into an i and the ending goes on after it.
feedback.feed_forward: Change y to i before you add the ending.

payload.context: Build one sentence about the three ways across the Verdon.

expected: the tunnel is the quickest of the three crossings

feedback.why_key: The small word goes in front of the ending, and the group being beaten follows straight after it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the in front of an -est ending, every time.

payload.given: The coast road takes fifty minutes. The bypass takes thirty-five.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that weighs the two roads against each other.

expected: is quicker than the coast road
is faster than the coast road
is quicker than the coast road by fifteen minutes

feedback.why_key: Two numbers collapse into one clause: the ending carries the comparison and than carries the road that lost.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the winner first, then add than.

payload.audio_text: The flat upstairs is bigger and it's warmer.

expected: the flat upstairs is bigger and it's warmer
the flat upstairs is bigger and its warmer
the flat upstairs is bigger and it is warmer

feedback.why_key: The endings are unstressed and easy to lose. Lose them and you hear one flat described rather than two flats weighed up.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the very end of the describing word.

payload.sentence: Evening classes are the most easiest option to fit round a shift pattern.

feedback.why_key: Easiest has already put the classes at the top of the group. Most is a second run at the same job.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete most when the word already ends in -est.

items.decision_cue: the most steeply of the six districts

payload.context: Two lines taken from separate notes on one set of figures.
sentences: Fares in Marlow rose more steeply than fares in Ashfield.
Fares in Marlow rose the most steeply of the six districts.
meanings: Two places are being weighed against each other, and one of them moved further.
Marlow sits at the top of a list of six, with nothing above it.

feedback.why_key: One sentence weighs a pair; the other ranks a group of six. The ending is the only thing telling you which.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask how many things are in the group before you choose the ending.

payload.prompt_text: A graph shows freight moved by road, rail and water over ten years. Road is highest all the way through and water is lowest. Write one sentence that ranks all three.

feedback.why_key: Ranking three things inside one sentence is the move that turns a list of numbers into a description of a graph.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the top, then place the other two against it.

payload.prompt_text: Open your freight graph answer. Rewrite the overview so that it ranks the three modes in a single sentence instead of listing them one after another. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: An overview that ranks is doing the task. An overview that lists is only reading the graph out loud.
feedback.feed_forward: Rank first, then give the numbers that prove the ranking.

points.title: Saying two things are level, or that one falls short of the other

point_json.grammar_name: as ... as, not as ... as, the same as, similar to, different from

teach.can_do: I can say that two things are level, or that one of them does not reach the other.
teach.why_it_matters: A description that only ever names winners cannot say two figures met, and figures meet constantly. These frames also keep a preposition each, and learners lose all three.
teach.meaning: A comparison does not always have a winner. Sometimes the whole point is that two things sit at the same height, and sometimes it is that one of them stops short of the other. English builds both with a frame rather than with an ending, and the describing word sits inside the frame without changing shape at all. That last part is what makes these easy to build, and it is also why they go wrong: the ending arrives out of habit and has nothing to do.

form.pattern: as + WORD + as  ·  not as + WORD + as  ·  the same as  ·  similar to  ·  different from
notes: the word inside the frame never changes shape: as high as, not as high as — never as higher as
the same needs the in front and one as after it: the fee is the same as last year's
similar always takes to; different always takes from
with things you count the frame stretches to as many ... as; with things you measure it is as much ... as
not so ... as turns up in speech, but not as ... as is safe everywhere and costs nothing
the frame can carry a whole noun phrase: as high a figure as, as long a wait as
form.negative: not as high as, or the gentler not quite as high as
form.question: Is the new pass as cheap as the old one?

worked_example.sentence: Rail carried as much freight in 2016 as it had ten years earlier.
worked_example.why_this_form: The two figures met, so there is no winner to name. The frame holds them side by side and leaves the describing word alone.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Carried more freight than would put 2016 in front, which the figures do not support, and it would hide the fact that a decade produced no movement at all.

notice_set.sentence: The new footbridge is not as wide as the old one.
notice_set.question: Which bridge takes more people side by side?
notice_set.why: Not as wide as stops the new bridge short of the old one, so the old one is the roomier of the two.

notice_set.sentence: Fees in Ashfield are the same as fees in Marlow.
notice_set.question: Would you pay more in Marlow?
notice_set.why: The same as sets the two towns at one figure, so neither of them is the dearer place.

notice_set.sentence: The pool is as busy on Sunday as it is on Saturday.
notice_set.question: Is Sunday the quiet day?
notice_set.why: The frame holds the two days at one level, so neither of them can be the quiet one.

notice_set.sentence: Water use in the south is similar to water use in the east.
notice_set.question: Are the two figures close together?
notice_set.why: Similar claims a short distance between the two. It does not claim there is none.

notice_set.sentence: Journey times on the coast route are nowhere near as reliable as they were.
notice_set.question: Has the route got worse?
notice_set.why: Nowhere near stretches the shortfall as far as it will go, and today's route is on the low end of it.

teach.rule_line: Two ases hold two things level. Put not in front and the first one falls short.
teach.false_rule: That this frame is only for things that are exactly equal. It measures the distance between two things, and one of the distances it measures is none.

errors.wrong: The tunnel is as quicker as the bypass in the evening.
errors.right: The tunnel is as quick as the bypass in the evening.
errors.why_it_happens: Every comparison the learner has built so far needed an ending, so the ending comes along automatically. Inside this frame there is nothing for it to do, because the frame is already doing the comparing.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two letters: quicker becomes quick.

errors.wrong: Rents in Marlow are different than rents in Brackenfield.
errors.right: Rents in Marlow are different from rents in Brackenfield.
errors.why_it_happens: Than is the word that follows every other comparison, so it turns up here as well. Different is not that kind of word and never has been: it takes from.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: than becomes from.

errors.wrong: This year's total is as same as last year's.
errors.right: This year's total is the same as last year's.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has one frame for comparing and pushes same into it. Same is an ordinary describing word that needs the in front of it, and only one as behind.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: the first as becomes the.

errors.wrong: The reserve gets as much visitors as the castle does.
errors.right: The reserve gets as many visitors as the castle does.
errors.why_it_happens: Much and many both mean a large amount and nothing in the meaning separates them, so whichever is nearer the front of the learner's mind goes in. Only many will sit in front of something you count one at a time.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: much becomes many.

pays_in.note: Half the sentences in a chart description report a level, not a winner.
pays_in.model: In 2014 the reserve drew as many visitors as the castle.

pays_in.note: Comparing where you live now with where you lived before.
pays_in.model: The new place isn't as noisy as the flat I had before.

pays_in.note: A statement that swaps from for than, or drops the second as, is testing exactly this.
pays_in.model: Rainfall in the uplands was similar to rainfall on the coast.

used_in.quote: Two towns with the same recycling figure cannot be described with a ranking, and the bar chart hands the learner several such pairs.
Part 3 answers about sport compare two activities or two generations, and most of those comparisons end level.

payload.sentence: The five-a-side pitch isn't as busy as it used to be.
payload.question: Do fewer people use it now?

feedback.why_key: The frame holds today's pitch below its own past, so use has come down since then.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the two things being held apart before you answer.

payload.sentence: Rainfall in the Verdon valley is similar to rainfall further inland.
payload.question: Are the two areas close on this measure?

feedback.why_key: Similar claims a short distance between two figures. It stops well short of claiming they match.
feedback.feed_forward: Read similar as close, never as equal.

payload.context: A draft paragraph on a table of district rents.
payload.sentence: Rents in Brackenfield are different than rents in Sandmouth.
reasons: different does not take than
the two districts cannot be weighed this way
the sentence is missing its second as
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Than belongs after an ending or after more. Different asks for from and will not take anything else.
feedback.feed_forward: Pair different with from before you write the second half.

payload.context: From a report weighing up two regions.
payload.stem: Water use in the south is ___ same as water use in the east.

feedback.why_key: Same is an ordinary describing word and needs the in front of it. An as will not do that job.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the same as as one three-word block.

payload.context: Two colleagues weighing up two places to eat near the depot.
payload.stem: The café gets as ___ customers at lunchtime as the canteen does.

feedback.why_key: Customers arrive one at a time and can be counted, so the frame takes many. Much is for what you measure instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether you could count them before choosing.

payload.given: Rail moved 40 million tonnes in 2006. Rail moved 40 million tonnes in 2016.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence saying the two years came out level.

expected: as much freight in 2016 as it did in 2006
as much freight in 2016 as in 2006
the same amount of freight in 2016 as in 2006
as much in 2016 as it did in 2006

feedback.why_key: Two identical figures have no winner between them. The frame sets them side by side and says so in one clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for the frame whenever two numbers match.

payload.context: Build one sentence about visitor numbers on the island.

expected: the island is not as popular as it was in 2010

feedback.why_key: Not sits in front of the whole frame, and the describing word stays plain between the two ases.
feedback.feed_forward: Put not before the frame, never inside it.

payload.audio_text: It's not as quiet as the place we had before.

expected: it's not as quiet as the place we had before
its not as quiet as the place we had before
it is not as quiet as the place we had before

feedback.why_key: Both ases are unstressed and the second almost disappears. Learners write not quiet as and lose half the frame.
feedback.feed_forward: Count two ases every time you hear this frame.

payload.sentence: The fee for an evening class is as same as the daytime fee.

feedback.why_key: Same needs the in front of it, and a single as behind is enough to carry the second half.
feedback.feed_forward: Change the first as to the whenever same follows.

payload.context: A paragraph arguing about the cost of keeping fit.
payload.sentence: Swimming at the council pool is as cheaper as running in the park.
reasons: the describing word should stay plain inside the frame
the two activities are too different to weigh
the sentence needs from instead of the second as
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The frame is already doing the comparing. An ending on top of it makes the sentence compare twice over.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip the ending off the word between the two ases.

payload.prompt_text: A chart shows household recycling in two towns. In 2018 both of them recycled 44 out of every hundred tonnes. Write one sentence reporting that, without naming a winner.

feedback.why_key: Figures meet all the time, and a writer with no way of saying so has to invent a difference that is not there.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the two are level, then give the year.

payload.prompt_text: Open your recycling chart answer. Find a place where two figures are level or nearly level, and rewrite that sentence so it reports the level instead of ranking them. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: Under time pressure every sentence turns into a ranking, and a reader who checks two of them stops trusting the rest.
feedback.feed_forward: Check each comparison for a winner that is not really there.

points.title: Putting something near the top without claiming it is the top

point_json.grammar_name: one of the + superlative + plural noun; among the most

teach.can_do: I can put something near the top of a group without claiming it is the very top.
teach.why_it_matters: A top-of-the-list claim needs only one counter-example to fall over, and it takes the rest of your paragraph with it. This frame keeps the claim strong and keeps it survivable.
teach.meaning: A top ranking is the strongest claim English will let you make about a group: nothing else comes close, and one exception destroys it. Most of the time what you actually mean is weaker and more useful — that the thing sits in the small handful at the top. That is what this frame says. Because it reaches into a group and picks one member out, the group itself has to be named, and a group is always more than one.

form.pattern: one of the + -est / most + PLURAL NOUN  ·  among the + -est / most + PLURAL NOUN
notes: the noun after the frame is always plural, because it names the group, not the thing: one of the largest towns
the verb answers to one, not to the plural: one of the busiest stations is closed this week
among the takes no one and no a in front of it: among the cheapest options available
a clause hanging off the plural noun agrees with the group: one of the few schemes that have survived
it works on words describing how something is done too: one of the most heavily used crossings
the softer versions: among the busier crossings, one of the more expensive options — near the top, no ranking claimed
form.negative: not one of the cheapest puts the thing outside the top group without saying where it does sit.
form.question: Is it one of the busiest crossings on the river?

spec.label: how strong is the claim, and how easily does it fall over?

steps.text: the busiest crossing on the river
steps.gloss: alone at the top; one busier crossing sinks the sentence

steps.text: one of the busiest crossings on the river
steps.gloss: in the top handful; survives a reader who knows the river
above the middle, and nothing more is claimed
no claim about anything else at all

worked_example.sentence: Sandmouth is one of the wettest towns on this stretch of coast.
worked_example.why_this_form: The claim is strong enough to be worth making and small enough to survive a reader who knows a wetter town. The group at the top has several members, so towns is plural.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The wettest town would stand Sandmouth alone at the top, and a single rainier place anywhere along that coast would make the whole sentence untrue.

notice_set.sentence: Brackenfield has one of the oldest markets in the county.
notice_set.question: Could any market in the county be older?
notice_set.why: The frame reaches into a small group at the top and picks one member, so a handful of older markets is exactly what it expects.

notice_set.sentence: Brackenfield has the oldest market in the county.
notice_set.question: Could any market in the county be older?
notice_set.why: Nothing is left above it, so one older market anywhere in the county would make the sentence untrue.

notice_set.sentence: Cycling is among the cheapest ways of getting into town.
notice_set.question: Might something be cheaper than cycling?
notice_set.why: Among places cycling inside the cheap group and deliberately leaves room underneath it.

notice_set.sentence: One of the two lifts is out of service today.
notice_set.question: How many lifts are working?
notice_set.why: The sentence picks a single lift out of the pair and says nothing at all against the other one.

notice_set.sentence: The island is one of the few places on this coast that have kept a daily boat.
notice_set.question: Do other places still have a daily boat?
notice_set.why: Few places names a small surviving group, and the island is one member of it rather than the whole of it.

teach.rule_line: One of the always lands on a group, so the thing you name after it must be plural.
teach.false_rule: That one of means you are describing one thing, so the noun should be singular. One picks the item; the noun names the group it was picked out of.

errors.wrong: Marlow is one of the largest town in the district.
errors.right: Marlow is one of the largest towns in the district.
errors.why_it_happens: One is sitting right beside the noun and drags it into the singular. The noun is not describing Marlow, though — it is naming the group Marlow has just been lifted out of.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: town becomes towns.

errors.wrong: One of the busiest crossings are closed for repairs.
errors.right: One of the busiest crossings is closed for repairs.
errors.why_it_happens: Crossings stands next to the verb and wins the argument by being nearest. The thing that is actually shut is a single crossing, and that is the word the verb has to answer to.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: are becomes is.

errors.wrong: Traffic is the most serious problem any council has to deal with.
errors.right: Traffic is one of the most serious problems any council has to deal with.
errors.why_it_happens: The unhedged version sounds more forceful, and force feels like a virtue in an argument. The reader only has to think of one worse problem to stop believing the paragraph.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert three words: one of the.

errors.wrong: It is one of the few schemes that has survived the cuts.
errors.right: It is one of the few schemes that have survived the cuts.
errors.why_it_happens: The clause looks as though it belongs to the one, but it is doing its work on schemes: the survivors are the few, and one of them is being singled out afterwards.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: has becomes have.

pays_in.note: It lets you make a strong claim you can still defend in the next sentence.
pays_in.model: Housing is one of the hardest costs for a young household to absorb.

pays_in.note: It ranks a bar without pretending it stands alone at the top.
pays_in.model: Rail was among the fastest-growing categories across the period.

pays_in.note: Part 3 runs on claims that are strong without being absolute.
pays_in.model: It's one of the reasons people move away, though it isn't the only one.

used_in.quote: An answer about services in small towns has to rank several problems, and every ranking in it needs to survive a reader who lives in one.
A statement that turns the passage's hedged ranking into an outright top ranking is false on those three small words.

payload.sentence: The Norland reserve is one of the largest wetlands in the region.
payload.question: Might another wetland in the region be about the same size?

feedback.why_key: The frame puts the reserve in the top handful and leaves the other members of that handful standing.
feedback.feed_forward: Read one of the as top handful, not as top.

payload.sentence: That's one of the better places to eat near the station.
payload.question: Is the speaker saying nowhere else nearby is any good?

feedback.why_key: The frame names a group of decent places and picks one out, so the rest of the group is still there.
feedback.feed_forward: Notice how much the speaker is not claiming.

items.decision_cue: one of the fastest growing city

payload.context: A draft paragraph about towns that have grown quickly.
payload.sentence: Ashfield is one of the fastest growing city in the north.
reasons: the group being named has to be plural
the ranking is stronger than the evidence allows
the sentence needs among instead of one of
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The word after the ending names the group Ashfield was picked from, and a group of one is not a group.
feedback.feed_forward: Make the noun plural whenever one of the comes first.

payload.context: From a paragraph on a table of district populations.
payload.stem: Ashfield is one of the fastest-growing ___ (district) in the county.

feedback.why_key: The word names the group Ashfield has been lifted out of, and that group has several members in it.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the plural ending after one of the.

payload.context: A notice at the Verdon river crossings.
payload.stem: One of the two river crossings ___ (be) shut until April.

feedback.why_key: A single crossing is shut. Crossings is only there to say which pair it came out of.
feedback.feed_forward: Look back to one before you choose the verb.

payload.given: The Verdon is the most polluted river in the region.

points.title: Saying how big the difference is, not just that there is one

point_json.grammar_name: Grading a comparison: far, much, slightly, considerably, marginally, nowhere near

teach.can_do: I can say how big a difference is, in one word, and get the size right.
teach.why_it_matters: A bare comparison tells the reader a difference exists and leaves them to guess whether it matters. The guess is usually wrong, and it is the difference between describing a chart and reading one aloud.
teach.meaning: A comparison on its own reports a direction: one thing is higher than another. It says nothing about distance, so two figures a whisker apart and two figures miles apart come out as the same sentence. A grading word puts the distance back in. It is one word, it goes in front of the comparison, and it decides whether the reader treats the gap as noise or as the story.

form.pattern: GRADER + comparative + than  ·  GRADER + as + WORD + as
notes: big gap: far, much, considerably, significantly, substantially, a great deal
small gap: slightly, marginally, a little, somewhat, a fraction
next to nothing: barely, hardly, no higher than, little more than
the grader always goes in front of the comparison, never after it
it works on both builds: much higher, and much more expensive
with the level frame the graders change shape: nowhere near as high as, almost as high as, just as high as, not quite as high as
very will not grade a comparison. Very high is fine; very higher is not
a lot, loads, way and miles belong to speech; considerably, substantially and marginally belong to writing, and mixing them up is visible on the page
form.negative: no higher than, not much higher than, nowhere near as high as
form.question: How much higher is it — a little, or a great deal?

spec.label: how big is the gap between the two figures?

steps.gloss: the two are not in the same conversation
level, or below; there is no gap to report
a gap you would need the table to see
visible, and not worth building anything on
a gap of unstated size — the reader has to guess
one of the things the chart is about

worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Far higher would promise a gap worth explaining, and the reader would go looking in the figures for something that is not there.

teach.rule_line: Look at the two numbers, then pick the one word that sizes the gap between them.
teach.false_rule: That dramatically, sharply and significantly make a description sound more academic. They make a claim about size, and the numbers underneath either back it or contradict it.

contrast.question: How big is the gap, and is the size worth saying?

a.means: A few pounds in it. Nobody would move house over the difference.

b.text: Rents in Marlow are far higher than rents in Ashfield.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote far higher for a two-pound gap. The sentence is correct English and wrong about the chart: your reader now pictures a gap the figures do not contain, and every number after it has to fight that picture.

edge_case.text: Very will not stretch a comparison — not very higher, not very more expensive. It strengthens the plain word instead: very high. Learn the pair much higher and very high together and the problem stops arising.

contrast.stronger_test: Cover the sentence and look only at the two numbers. If you had to describe the gap to somebody over the phone in a single word, which word would come out? That is the one the sentence needs.

errors.why_it_happens: Very is the word the learner reaches for to make anything stronger, and it has never failed them before. It will strengthen a plain describing word, but it cannot stretch a comparison.

points.title: Saying that when one thing changes, another changes with it

teach.can_do: I can say that two things move together, and which way each of them goes.
teach.why_it_matters: It packs a whole cause-and-effect sentence into eight words, and it is one of the few patterns that reads as fluent even when the rest of the paragraph is plain.
teach.meaning: Two things are moving, and they are tied to each other: whenever one goes up, the other follows it up or pulls the other way. Two separate sentences would report both movements and leave the reader to guess whether there is a link. This pattern states the link itself, and it does it without a single word for cause. The shape carries the meaning, which is why the shape has to be exact.

form.pattern: The + comparison + first half, the + comparison + second half
notes: both halves open with the, and the comparison jumps to the front of its own half: the longer the wait, the angrier the queue
in short halves the verb is often left out entirely: the sooner the better
the two halves have to be built the same way — a full clause on the left wants a full clause on the right
when a noun is involved the whole phrase moves forward: the more money a council spends, the fewer complaints it receives
use fewer with things you count and less with things you measure: the fewer complaints, the less paperwork
increasingly does a smaller version of the same job on one scale by itself: journeys are increasingly made by rail
increasingly goes in front of the word it stretches: increasingly crowded, increasingly hard to fund
form.negative: The less you book ahead, the more you pay — the pattern reverses simply by changing the comparison in either half.
form.question: Does one really move with the other, or do they just both happen to be moving?

left.text: the longer the wait at the clinic

right.text: the more people give up and go home

spec.caption: Two scales tied together. The pattern claims the tie; two separate sentences would only report the two movements.

worked_example.sentence: The later the train leaves, the fewer connections there are at the other end.
worked_example.why_this_form: Every extra minute takes another connection away, so the two are tied rather than merely both true. The sentence states the tie in one clause pair.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Two separate sentences would report a late train and a thin timetable and leave the reader to work out for themselves whether one of them causes the other.

teach.rule_line: Two halves, each opening with the, each with its comparison pulled to the front.
teach.false_rule: That the here is the ordinary little word that goes in front of a noun. It is a different word doing a different job, and it turns up twice or not at all.

errors.wrong: The more the council spends, the less complaints it receives.
errors.right: The more the council spends, the fewer complaints it receives.
errors.why_it_happens: Less is the word that comes out when the meaning is downwards, and it works in front of almost everything the learner says out loud. Complaints arrive one at a time, and that is the one thing less will not sit in front of.

errors.wrong: The busier the road, the more accidents happening.

errors.wrong: The centre of town is becoming crowded increasingly.
errors.right: The centre of town is becoming increasingly crowded.
errors.why_it_happens: Words ending in -ly usually settle at the end of a clause, and this one is treated the same way. It belongs in front of whatever it is stretching, exactly like the other size words.

points.title: Saying how many times bigger one figure is than another

point_json.grammar_name: twice as many, three times higher, more than double, a tenfold increase

teach.can_do: I can say how many times one figure fits into another, and get the direction right.
teach.why_it_matters: A chart description that can only report differences has to give every number twice. A multiple says the relationship once, in three words, and a reader who never sees the chart still gets it.
teach.meaning: There are two honest ways of describing the distance between two figures. One is the difference: subtract the smaller from the larger and report what is left. The other is the multiple: ask how many times the smaller one fits into the larger, and report that. They answer different questions. A difference of two hundred is enormous between two figures of three hundred and meaningless between two figures of a million, and a multiple carries its own scale with it.

form.pattern: twice / three times + as + many / much / WORD + as  ·  NUMBER times + comparative + than  ·  a NUMBERfold increase
notes: twice, not two times, in careful writing. From three upwards the number is used: three times, four times
as many with things you count, as much with things you measure: twice as many visitors, twice as much rain
the second half takes as after as high, and than after higher — three times as high as, or three times higher than, and never a mixture of the two
double and half attach straight to the noun: double the number of visitors, half the rainfall
the noun versions: a twofold increase, a threefold rise, a tenfold increase — written as one word, with the number spelt out
the verbs: double, treble, halve — demand doubled between 2005 and 2015
hedges go in front, not inside: almost twice as many, just over three times higher, more than double
form.negative: half as many as sends the multiple the other way, and so does a halving of.
form.question: How many times does the smaller figure fit into the larger one?

right.text: twice as many visitors as the castle

points.title: Saying how a figure moved, how far it went and where it ended up

point_json.grammar_name: The grammar of change: rise in / rise to / rise by, from ... to, peak at, level off
signal_blocklist: as can be seen from the graph

teach.can_do: I can describe how a figure moved: how far it travelled, where it stopped and what shape the journey had.
teach.why_it_matters: A chart description is nothing but this. Every sentence reports a movement, and the small word after the verb is where the marks go.
teach.meaning: A chart hands you two kinds of number and English keeps them apart. One is the movement itself, which is how far the line travelled. The other is the level, which is where it stopped. The verb names the shape of the journey and the small word after it tells the reader which of those two numbers is coming next. Choose the right verb and the wrong preposition, and the reader still walks away with a different chart from the one in front of you.

form.pattern: rise / fall + by SIZE  ·  rise / fall + to LEVEL  ·  rise / fall + from START + to END  ·  a rise / fall + in WHAT  ·  a rise / fall + of SIZE  ·  peak / stand / remain + at LEVEL
notes: The three prepositions do three different jobs. By measures the movement: rose by four points. To names the level it reached: rose to eleven per cent. In names the thing that is moving: a rise in unemployment.
The verb takes by for the size; the noun takes of for the size and never by. Output fell by nine million. There was a fall of nine million.
from ... to ... gives both ends at once and wants nothing else with it: demand rose from twenty to thirty-five million litres.

The irregular past forms, which are the ones that get guessed: rise / rose / risen, fall / fell / fallen, grow / grew / grown. The rest are regular: increase, decrease, decline, double, fluctuate, plateau, peak.
rise never takes an object and never goes passive; raise does both. Prices rose. The council raised the fee. Never was risen, and never was increased when nobody did the increasing.
Verb and noun come in fixed pairs: rise / a rise, fall / a fall, grow / growth (there is no a grow), decline / a decline, fluctuate / a fluctuation, level off / a levelling off, peak / a peak.
The flat verbs report an absence of movement and take no figure at all: level off, plateau, remain stable, hold steady, fluctuate. Only peak, stand and remain take at.

Adverb after the verb, adjective in front of the noun, and they come in matched pairs: rose sharply / a sharp rise, fell dramatically / a dramatic fall, grew steadily / steady growth, dipped slightly / a slight dip.
The article is not optional in the noun version. There was a sharp rise, never there was sharp rise. Growth is the exception, because it is uncountable: steady growth, no article.
form.negative: The negative you almost never need is nothing fell. Reach instead for the flat verbs — remained stable, showed little change, held steady at — which say it without a negative.
form.question: Which number am I about to give: how far it moved, or where it ended up?

left.text: demand fell by nine million litres

right.text: demand fell to nine million litres

spec.caption: Same verb, same figure, two different charts. One small word is the only thing telling the reader which one you are looking at.

worked_example.sentence: Industrial water demand rose by a fifth between 2000 and 2010, peaking at just over ninety million litres a day.
worked_example.why_this_form: By measures the climb and at fixes the highest point. Two numbers doing two different jobs, and neither preposition will do the other one's work.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Rose to a fifth would put demand at twenty per cent of something. That is a level, not a climb, and it describes a different graph.

notice_set.sentence: Unemployment in the northern districts fell by four per cent between 2010 and 2014.
notice_set.question: What was unemployment in 2014?
options: four per cent lower than in 2010
notice_set.why: By measures the drop and nothing else. Without the 2010 figure there is no way to work out where it landed.

notice_set.sentence: Unemployment in the northern districts fell to four per cent by 2014.
notice_set.question: What was unemployment in 2014?
options: four per cent lower than in 2010
notice_set.why: To names the level the line stopped at, so four per cent is the destination rather than the distance travelled.

notice_set.sentence: Visitor numbers levelled off after 2016.
notice_set.question: Did visitor numbers go down after 2016?
notice_set.why: Levelling off is a line that stops moving. It is flat, not falling, and that is exactly why the verb exists.

notice_set.sentence: Rainfall in the catchment fluctuated between 2005 and 2012.
notice_set.question: Did rainfall end the period higher than it started it?
notice_set.why: Fluctuate reports repeated movement up and down and makes no claim at all about the two end points.

notice_set.sentence: Household spending on fuel peaked at eleven per cent in 2013.
notice_set.question: Was eleven per cent the highest figure anywhere in the period?
notice_set.why: A peak is the top of the whole graph, not just a local bump, and at pins it to one number.

notice_set.sentence: There was a slight rise in cycling, followed by a dramatic fall.
notice_set.question: Which of the two movements was the bigger one?
notice_set.why: Slight and dramatic are the two words carrying the sizes, and they sit in front of the nouns rather than after the verbs.

teach.rule_line: Ask which number is coming: how far it moved, or the level it reached.
teach.false_rule: That the little word after a change verb is decoration, so by, to, in and of are interchangeable. Each one points the reader at a different number.

errors.wrong: There was a sharp rise of unemployment in the northern districts after 2009.
errors.right: There was a sharp rise in unemployment in the northern districts after 2009.
errors.why_it_happens: Of is the all-purpose linking word and it arrives first. The learner has also met a rise of nine points, which is correct, and does not yet separate the thing that rises from the size of the rise.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: of becomes in.

errors.wrong: Freight moved by rail fell by nine million tonnes, a drop by almost a third.
errors.right: Freight moved by rail fell by nine million tonnes, a drop of almost a third.
errors.why_it_happens: By was correct three words earlier, so it is still loaded and fires again. The verb takes by for the size of a movement; the noun for that same movement takes of.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: the second by becomes of.

errors.wrong: A dramatically fall in rainfall followed the diversion of the river.
errors.right: A dramatic fall in rainfall followed the diversion of the river.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has drilled fell dramatically and stored the pair as one lump. Turning the verb into a noun leaves the adverb behind, and nothing in the meaning signals that it has to change shape too.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two letters: dramatically becomes dramatic.

errors.wrong: Visitor numbers rose between 2005 and 2010 sharply.
errors.right: Visitor numbers rose sharply between 2005 and 2010.
errors.why_it_happens: The dates feel like the important information, so they go straight after the verb and the adverb is left to trail on the end. English wants the manner word next to the verb it describes.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: sharply goes straight after rose.

errors.wrong: Rainfall in the uplands was decreased steadily after 2011.
errors.right: Rainfall in the uplands decreased steadily after 2011.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught that the passive makes a description sound academic and applies it to a verb that has no object to promote. Nobody decreased the rainfall; it went down on its own.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: was.
